items: Running git clean -f without the same command with -n first. Root cause: untracked files were never objects, so no reflog, fsck or stash can bring them back.
Using -x where -d was meant. Root cause: -x adds ignored paths, which is where .env files, datasets and checkpoints usually are.
Assuming a plain git stash push took the new files. Root cause: without -u an entry holds changes to tracked files only.
Running git stash drop straight after a conflicted pop "because pop did not". Root cause: pop skipped the drop on purpose; the entry is the only complete copy until the conflict is resolved.
Keeping a week of work in the stash. Root cause: an entry is reachable only from refs/stash, is not pushed, not shown by git log, and one drop or clear removes its only ref.

beats.text: They open the reflog, Git's local record of where each ref has been. Nothing. They run git fsck, which lists objects that nothing reaches. Nothing. They ask you which command brings the files back.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Two commands today, and they sit at opposite ends of the undo map.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Two commands today, and they sit at opposite ends of the undo map.

beats.text: git clean deletes untracked files. It's the only undo in Git whose effect nothing in Git can reverse.
beats.tele: `git clean` deletes untracked files. It's the only undo in Git whose effect nothing in Git can reverse.

beats.text: git stash does nearly the opposite. It takes uncommitted work, turns it into commits, and clears your working tree, so that the work can come back later. Because the work becomes objects, almost everything about stash is recoverable, including an entry you dropped by mistake.

beats.text: What it changes: the working tree only. It deletes untracked paths, and ignored ones too with -x or -X.

beats.text: What it can destroy: anything Git doesn't track: notebooks, results, .env files, datasets, checkpoints.

beats.text: Stash. In one sentence: git stash push 🟡 CAUTION records the index and the working tree as commits that only refs/stash reaches, then resets both to HEAD, so that the work can be brought back later, on this commit or on another.
beats.tele: Stash. In one sentence: `git stash push` 🟡 CAUTION records the index and the working tree as commits that only `refs/stash` reaches, then resets both to HEAD, so that the work can be brought back later, on this commit or on another.

beats.text: Precisely. A stash entry is a commit whose tree is the state of your tracked files. Its first parent is the commit that was HEAD, and its second parent records the index. With -u, a third parent holds the untracked files. refs/stash points at the newest entry, and older entries live in the reflog of that ref, hence the names stash@{1}, stash@{2}.
beats.tele: Precisely. A stash entry is a commit whose tree is the state of your tracked files. Its first parent is the commit that was HEAD, and its second parent records the index. With `-u`, a third parent holds the untracked files. `refs/stash` points at the newest entry, and older entries live in the reflog of that ref, hence the names `stash@{1}`, `stash@{2}`.

beats.text: git stash apply merges the entry's changes into the current files. git stash pop is apply followed by drop, and the drop happens only if the apply succeeded.

beats.text: There are two ways on. One: resolve the file, clear the conflict state with git restore --staged or git add, and drop the entry yourself. git stash drop 🔴 DANGEROUS: it deletes the only ref to work that was never committed. Appropriate only when the entry's content is committed elsewhere, or on disk as here, or you want none of it.
